notes: West leads the ♠9 against 3NT. South has only 6 top tricks (3 spades, 2 hearts, and the ♦A). 3 extra tricks could be taken in diamonds if the finesse works. Dummy's 3 entries mean that even if East has 4 diamonds to the King the suit can still be picked up.

If the diamond finesse fails, however, the contract will be in trouble. South will not have time to establish the clubs as the defense will be able to cash enough spades to set the contract by the time that suit is established.

South can make his contract regardless of the position of the ♦K by playing clubs at tricks 2 and 4. The defense has no way to prevent South from establishing enough club tricks to ensure the contract.

review.hl: ND5 ND4 ND3 ND2 SDA SDQ SDJ SDT
NCQ NCJ NCT NC9 NC8 NC7
EST ES5 ES4 ES3 ES2 WS8 WS7 WS6
NCQ NCJ NCT NC9 NC8 NC7 SC3 SC2
NCQ NCJ NCT NC9 NC8 NC7

notes: West leads the ♣8 against 6NT. South has 11 top tricks (the ♠A, 3 each in hearts and diamonds, and 4 clubs). South must look towards spades for trick number 12.

After winning the opening lead, South should lead a spade intending to play the ♠9 from dummy if West follows low. Hopefully, West will have the ♠10 and at least 1 of the ♠K and ♠Q. On the given lie of the cards East wins the ♠K.
South wins the return in hand. He leads another spade, playing the ♠J when West follows low. If all goes according to plan, the ♠J will hold and South will have 12 tricks.

The alternative plan, leading a low spade to the ♠J will work only if West has both the ♠K and ♠Q. This plan is inferior to the recommended line as it requires West to have 2 specific cards (the ♠K and ♠Q). The recommended line only requires West having 1 specific card (the ♠10) and at least 1 of 2 other cards (the ♠K and ♠Q).

review.hl: NHK NHQ NHJ SHA SH3 SH2
NDA NDQ NDJ SDK SD3 SD2
NSA NSJ NS9 SS4 SS3 SS2

notes: After the defense takes the first 3 heart tricks, and exits a club, South must take the balance. South's only concern is to avoid losing a trick to the ♠K. After drawing trump, South will be able to trump his ♦2 in the dummy.
South could cash the ♠A. This play would work when either defender has a singleton ♠K (2 cases).

South could instead finesse West for the ♠K, leading spades from South and playing low from dummy if West doesn't play the ♠K. This plan will work when West has either the singleton ♠K, doubleton ♠K6, doubleton ♠K7, or tripleton ♠K (4 cases).
The percentage play is, therefore, to take the spade finesse. When you have a 10 card fit, containing all the high cards except the King, finessing against the King is the percentage play.

review.hl: EHA EHT EH9 EH8 WHK WHQ WHJ
NSA NS5 NS4 NS3 NS2 SSQ SSJ SST SS9 SS8

notes: After the defense cashes 2 spade tricks and the ♦A , South gains the lead in clubs. His only concern is to find the ♥K.
On the above lie of the cards, South can only pick up the hearts by dropping East's singleton ♥K. If West has both outstanding hearts, however, he must be finessed for the ♥K.
Playing for the drop is actually the percentage play. When you have an 11 card fit missing the King, play for the drop, don't finesse. A 1-1 break is more likely than a 2-0 break.

review.hl: ESQ ESJ EST ES9 WSA WSK WS8 WS7
NHA NH6 NH5 NH4 NH3 NH2 SHQ SHJ SHT SH9 SH8

notes: West leads the ♠7 against 3NT. South appears to have at least 10 tricks (2 or 3 in spades, the ♥A, 6 diamond tricks, and the ♣A). The blockage in the diamond suit could spell trouble if that suit is 4-1.

In order to cater to this possibility, South must win the ♠A at trick 1. South cashes his ♦A and ♦Q. South then gives up a trick to the ♠K. South can win any return and reach dummy's diamond suit with the newly created spade entry.
If South had won the first trick in dummy, the above position would result after South unblocks the diamonds. South would have no way to get to dummy's remaining diamonds and the contract would fail.

review.hl: NSQ NSJ NST SSA SS3 SS2
NDK NDJ ND5 ND4 ND3 ND2 SDA SDQ
NDK NDJ ND5 ND4 ND3 ND2 SDA SDQ

notes: West leads a trump against 4♥, which South wins in hand. South must lose a trick to the ♠A and the ♣A. South thus must find a way to dispose of one of his 2 diamond losers.

If West holds the ♦K, a simple finesse in that suit will solve South's problems. If that finesse loses, South will be in trouble. The defense will continue hearts, drawing another of North's trumps. A diamond is now played to North's ♦A with the hope of ruffing South's remaining diamond loser.

Now declarer must lead either a spade or a club from the dummy. The defense will take the ♠A or ♣A and lead a third round of hearts exhausting North's trumps and leaving South with a certain diamond loser.

South can give himself a much better chance by simply cashing the ♦A and playing the ♦Q, conceding a trick to the ♦K. As the diamond suit is now unblocked, South can win the trump continuation and ruff his last diamond in the dummy. South concedes the ♠A and ♣A, drawing the last trump as soon as he can.
South must lose tricks to the ♦A and the ♣A. West's heart lead has created 2 heart losers.
South must try to dispose of his 2 heart losers immediately. If South leads either diamonds or clubs first, West will win and cash the setting tricks in hearts.

South can discard 1 of his heart losers on dummy's top spades. However, one discard is not enough. South must risk the spade finesse. South leads low to dummy's ♠J at trick 2, playing West for the ♠Q. When that finesse works, South can get rid of both of his heart losers on North's ♠A and ♠K. South thus makes his contract losing tricks to only the ♦A and ♣A.

review.hl: NDT SDK SDQ SDJ SD9 SD8 SD7 SD6
NCK NCQ NCJ NCT NC9 SC3 SC2

notes: West leads the ♣Q against 7NT. Outside of spades there are 8 top tricks (4 hearts, 2 diamonds, and 2 clubs). After winning the opening club lead, South is faced with the problem of playing spades for 5 tricks. This will only pose a problem if one defender has 4 or more spades to the ♠J.
If West has length in spades, South could pick up the spade suit by passing the ♠10 through West. This would be a poor play as it would lose to more common spade holdings with the ♠J in East's hand.

South should thus gear his play towards guarding against East being long in spades. In order to deal with East having all 5 spades, South should cash the ♠A first. When West shows out, South can finesse against East's ♠J, cross to the ♥A, and finesse again.

If West follows to the first round of spades, North wins the ♠A. Another spade is lead to the ♠K or ♠Q in South's hand. If West shows out, South can cross to the ♥A. Only 1 spade finesse is needed in this case.

NHA NH2 SHK SHQ SHJ SHT
NSA NS3 NS2 SSK SSQ SST SS9 SS8
NSA NS3 NS2 SSK SSQ SST SS9 SS8

notes: West leads the ♥7 against 3NT. South appears to have 9 easy tricks (the ♥A, 3 diamond tricks, and 5 club tricks). South should win the opening lead as the defenders may be able to run the spades if South ducks.

Now, as long as clubs are breaking no worse than 3-1, 9 tricks look easy. There is only 1 pitfall. South must save his ♣2 for the fourth round of that suit to make sure the clubs don't get blocked. In the above position, South has played his ♣2 on 1 of the first 3 rounds of the suit. South can now take only 4 club tricks.
By saving his ♣2, 9 tricks become easy as all 5 of dummy's clubs can be enjoyed.

ESQ ESJ ES7 WSA WST WS9 WS8
NCA NCK NCQ NC5 NC4 SC8 SC7 SC6 SC2

notes: West leads the ♥K to dummy's ♥A. There are only 6 top tricks (the ♠A, the ♥A, and 4 diamond tricks). If the lead is lost in trying to establish club tricks the defense will be able to cash enough heart tricks to defeat the contract.
South must hope that East has the ♠K and finesse him for that card. The 3 extra spade tricks will be enough for the contract. As dummy only has one entry, the spades must be played carefully.

If East has four or more spades to the ♠K, and the ♠Q is led from the dummy, East will not cover. If the ♠3 is played by South the suit is blocked and only one more finesse can be taken when two more are needed. If South tries to unblock the spades by playing the ♠10 or ♠J under North's ♠Q, East will cover North's ♠9 with the ♠K and develop a sure stopper with his remaining ♠8 and ♠7.

South does better by playing the ♠9 the first time and underplaying with his ♠3 when East doesn't cover. The lead will remain in the dummy and the ♠Q is played next. If East ducks again, the lead remains in the North hand to take a third spade finesse.

review.hl: NC5 NC4 NC3 NC2 SCK SCQ SCJ
EH8 EH7 EH6 WHQ WHJ WHT WH9
NSQ NS9 NS2 SSA SSJ SST SS3

notes: West leads the ♠8 to East's ♠10 and South's ♠J. Declarer has 7 top tricks (1 spade, thanks to the lead, and 2 each in hearts, diamonds, and clubs). 2 additional tricks are available in clubs if that suit is 3-2. The ♦K will provide the entry to the long clubs.
In order to establish the long club tricks, South must first lose a trick in clubs. South would much rather lose the lead to West than to East.
If West is on lead, the defense will not be able to run the spade suit. With East on lead, however, one lead through South's fragile spade holding could spell disaster if West has five or six spades.
South should gear his play towards giving up the unavoidable club loser to West. South can always accomplish this if West has any 3 clubs by cashing the ♣A, ♣K, and giving up a club.

Declarer can also succeed when West has a doubleton ♣Q of clubs. South should lead a club towards dummy at trick 2. If West plays the ♣Q, South lets him hold that trick. If West follows low, South should win the ♣A and cross back to his hand.
South plays another club towards dummy, again ducking if West plays the ♣Q. If West follows small again, South should win the ♣K and give up a club trick, hoping that West began with 3 clubs.
This technique described in the club suit is from a family of plays called avoidance play. Avoidance play is characterized by steps taken to keep a dangerous opponent (in this case East) off lead.

review.hl: NCA NCK NDK SDA SHA SHK
NCA NCK NC7 NC6 NC5 NDK
NH5 NH4 NH3 SHA SHK SH2

notes: South has 12 top tricks (3 spades, the ♥A, the ♦A, and 7 club tricks). North's ♠10 is the only hope for a thirteenth trick.

After winning the opening lead and drawing trump, South must decide on how to play spades. South could cash the ♠A, ♠K, and ♠Q hoping that the ♠J drops, making the ♠10 high. Alternatively, South could play West for the ♠J, finessing the ♠10.

Finessing the ♠10 is in fact the percentage play. The finesse is necessary when West has the ♠J and length in the suit. Playing for the drop is necessary when East has the ♠J and shortness in the suit. Since the ♠J is more likely to be with length than with shortness, South should finesse.
A top honour in spades should be cashed first in case East has a singleton ♠J.

NCA NC4 NC3 SCK SCQ SCJ SC9 SC8 SC7 SC6

notes: After ruffing the opening heart lead, South's main concern is to play the trump suit for only one loser. The ♠K and ♠Q will always provide at least one trick for the defenders. South must play the suit to maximize the chance for only 1 loser.

South should cross to the dummy in diamonds (crossing in clubs is more likely to lead to a defensive ruff) and finesse in spades. On the above lie of the cards, South will immediately succeed. It would have done East no good to split his honours when North led a spade.

If the first spade finesse loses, South should ruff the heart return, cross to dummy again, this time in clubs, and take a second finesse in spades. If this finesse wins, South can draw the last trump with the ♠A and easily take the balance of the tricks.

notes: South has 8 top tricks (3 spade tricks, 2 heart tricks, and 3 club tricks). South can develop the diamond suit for his game going trick once the ♦A and ♦K are knocked out.

If South wins the opening lead and attacks diamonds, the contract will be in jeopardy when hearts are 5-2 and the diamond ♦A and ♦K are split. East will win the first diamond trick and clear the hearts. West will still have a diamond entry to cash out the heart suit.

South can guard against this distribution by allowing West to hold the opening lead. West will continue hearts, but when East wins the first diamond lead he will have no hearts left to lead. When West wins his diamond trick, South will still have a heart stopper.

review.hl: NCK NCQ NSA NSK SCA SHA SHK SSQ
ND5 ND4 ND3 ND2 SDQ SDJ SDT SD9
EDA EH6 WDK WHJ WHT WH9 WH8

notes: South has 8 top tricks (2 spade tricks, 2 heart tricks, and 4 club tricks). The ninth trick can eventually come from diamonds once the ♦A and ♦K are knocked out.

At first glance, it appears that South should allow West to win the first heart trick. If West has 5 hearts and the ♦A and ♦K are split, this hold up play will effectively shut out the defensive heart potential.
Unfortunately, the defense has even more potential in spades. West will not continue hearts, but will shift to spades. The contract will then have almost no chance of making.
South cannot make his contract on the above lie of the cards. He should not risk his contract (by playing the ♥2) when hearts were dealt 4-3 or when East was dealt 2 hearts and both the ♦A and ♦K.
South should win the opening lead and play on diamonds, hoping for a favorable lie of the cards, as above.

ND5 ND4 ND3 ND2 SDQ SDJ SDT SD9
EDA WDK WHJ WHT WH9 WH8
ND5 ND4 ND3 ND2 SDQ SDJ SDT SD9

notes: After winning the opening lead, South's only problem is not losing 2 trump tricks. South does have 2 heart losers, but Dummy's clubs can eventually be used to take care of those losers.

South has an almost certain way of playing the spade suit for only 1 loser. South should cash the ♠A or ♠K. When both defenders follow small, South should lead a low spade towards the ♠J in dummy. This plan will always work unless West was dealt all 5 spades. If East has all 5 spades the second round of spades must come from the dummy.

On the above distribution, for example, West will show out on the second spade lead towards the ♠J. East will win the ♠Q, but a finessing position exists over East's ♠10. After drawing trump, South can discard his heart losers on North's clubs.

review.hl: NSJ NS3 NS2 SSA SSK SS9 SS8 SS7
NCA NCQ NCJ NCT SHK SH4 SH3 SH2
NSJ NS3 NS2 SSA SSK SS9 SS8 SS7
NS3 EST ES6 SSA SS9 SS8
NCA NCQ NCJ NCT SHK SH4 SH3 SH2

notes: South has 5 top tricks outside of clubs (1 trick in spades and 2 tricks each in hearts and diamonds). If West has the ♣K, 5 club tricks can be taken by finessing in that suit.

If East has the ♣K, only 4 tricks will be available in clubs. 4 club tricks will still be enough for the contract, but the defense may be in a position to run the spades. If South wins the opening lead and East has the ♣K, that indeed will happen.
Upon winning the ♣K East will return a spade through South's remaining honour. West will be able to run the entire suit.

The bidding marks the winning line. West is known to have 6 spades to the ♠A for his opening weak 2 bid. If South allows West to hold the opening lead, the defense is left without recourse. If West continues spades, East will have no spades left upon winning the ♣K.

If West switches to hearts at trick 2, South can win and play on clubs. East may continue hearts, but South can hold up once. East clears the hearts, but when West wins the ♠A, he will have no hearts to play and South will have his 9 tricks.

review.hl: NDK NHK SDA SHA SSK SSQ SS2
NCA NCT NC9 NC8 NC7 SCQ SCJ SC2 WCK WC4
NCA NCT NC9 NC8 NC7 ECK EC6 EC5 SCQ SCJ SC2
ES6 ES5 WSA WSJ WST WS9 WS8 WS7
WSA WSJ WST WS9 WS8 WS7
NCA NCT NC9 NC8 NC7 SCQ SCJ SC2

notes: West leads the ♦J to his East's ♦A. East returns a diamond which South wins. South has already lost a trick to the ♦A and has 2 certain spade losers. South must therefore play the heart suit for no losers. South must find the ♥Q.

It is a well known fact that when holding 8 cards in a suit containing all of the honours except the Queen, one should generally finesse against that card. Many players holding the above combination would make the mistake of cashing the ♥A or ♥K before taking a second round heart finesse. This plan will fail when East has 4 hearts to the ♥Q.

The above line of play will succeed when West has a singleton ♥Q. As there are 4 small hearts and only 1 ♥Q outstanding, a singleton heart with West is four times more likely to be a small one. South can guard against this distribution by crossing to dummy and taking a first round trump finesse.
When that finesse wins, South can cross to dummy and finesse trumps again. The ♥A and ♥K will draw East's last 2 trumps. South concedes 2 spade tricks to the defense.

NH3 SHA SHK SHT SH9 SH8
NSQ NSJ NST NS9 NS8 SS3 SS2

notes: South should win the opening lead as he may have to lose a diamond trick. South has 8 top tricks (2 spades, 3 hearts, and 3 clubs) outside of diamonds. South can afford to lose a trick in diamonds. South should thus gear his play towards maximizing his chances of losing only 1 diamond trick.

If South starts by leading a diamond to dummy's ♦10 or ♦Q, East may win cheaply leaving South with a critical guess on the second round of the suit. Should South finesse again or play for the drop of the outstanding honour?
South can avoid this dilemma by taking North's ♦A on the first round of the suit. If both defenders follow small, South can return to his hand to play another diamond towards the dummy.
By playing diamonds in this way, South will succeed unless East has 3 or more diamonds including the ♦K and ♦J. In this case, the contract cannot be made.

NDA NDQ ND9 ND8 ND7 SD4 SD3
NHA NHQ NHJ SHK SH3 SH2

notes: South might as well cover the ♠J with the ♠Q at trick 1. Unfortunately, East can cover with the ♠K. South should win the ♠A.
South has finessing possibilities in both clubs and diamonds. If South takes a ruffing finesse in diamonds he can guarantee the contract.

South should begin by drawing trump. South next plays his ♦2 to the ♦A. Another diamond is played from dummy, South discarding the ♠2 if East doesn't cover. West can win the ♦K, but dummy will have plenty of diamond winners for South's club discards. The ♣A acts as an entry to those tricks.

review.hl: NCA NC5 NDA NDQ NDJ NDT ND9 ND8 SCQ SCJ SCT SC9 SD2
NDA NDQ NDJ NDT ND9 ND8 SHA SHK SHQ SHJ SHT SH9
NH4 NH3 NH2 SHA SHK SHQ SHJ SHT SH9
NDJ NDT ND9 ND8 SCQ SCJ SCT SC9

notes: The opening lead has created 2 possible diamond losers for South. South must find a way to dispose of his second diamond loser. West has shown a 6 card diamond suit with his weak 2 bid. East will thus be able to overruff the dummy if South tries to dispose of his second diamond loser in this way.
A better plan is to use dummy's club suit to take care of 1 of South's diamond losers. The following plan will work whenever clubs are no worse than 4-2 and trumps are 3-2.
South should win the opening lead (ducking the opening lead is also OK) and draw 3 rounds of trump. South next cashes dummy's ♣A and ♣K and trumps a club in his hand.
If clubs are 3-3, South has 2 discards for his diamond losers and can make an overtrick. If a defender shows out on the third round of clubs, South crosses in hearts and ruffs another club.
North will have a club winner established. South crosses in hearts and discards a diamond loser on North's good club. South concedes a diamond trick at the end.

review.hl: WDK WDQ WDJ WDT WD9 WD8
NSQ NS6 NS5 ESJ ES8 ES7
ECJ ECT EC9 EC8 WCQ WC7
NSQ NS6 NS5 SSA SSK SS4 SS3 SS2
NHK NHQ NHJ SHA SH3 SH2

notes: West leads the ♠Q which South wins. South has 8 top tricks (2 in spades, 4 in hearts, and 2 in clubs). South has finessing positions in both diamonds and clubs.

It is important that South takes the diamond finesse before the club finesse. If South takes the club finesse first and it loses, East will clear the spades. If West has 5 or more spades, South will no longer be able to take advantage of the ♦A being onside. West will take his ♦A and cash out the spades.

If South leads a diamond to the ♦K at trick 2 and that finesse loses, South will still be able to make his contract when West has the ♣Q. East will clear spades, but South can take 9 tricks, via the club finesse, without losing the lead.

NDK NDT ND3 ND2 SD7 SD6 SD5 SD4
NCK NCJ NC4 SCA SC3 SC2
NCK NCJ NC4 SCA SC3 SC2

notes: West leads the ♥J which South wins. South's only possible losers are in the trump suit. South should try to draw trump as quickly as possible. If spades break 3-2, no special technique is required. South can start by leading the ♠K, ♠Q, or ♠J out of his hand.
If West has 4 spades to the ♠A, nothing can be done. West will always get 2 trump tricks.
If East has 4 spades to the ♠A, South should be able to play trumps for 1 loser by leading spades from dummy towards South's holding three times, if necessary.

South should be careful in getting to dummy to lead spades. South must take steps to minimize the possibility of a defensive ruff. Suppose South crosses in diamonds first and plays a spade to an honour in the closed hand. If South crosses again in diamonds, the defense may be able to get a diamond ruff when the ♠A is won.

South should cross in clubs on either the first or second trip to the dummy. A defensive ruff is now considerably less likely. South plays spades again towards his hand. If West shows out, South can cross in diamonds and repeat the spade finesse a third time.

review.hl: WHJ WHT WH9 WH8 WH7 WH6

NS6 NS5 NS4 NS3 SSK SSQ SSJ SS2
NDA NDK ND4 SDQ SD3 SD2
NCA NC4 NC3 SCK SCQ SC2
NS6 NS5 NS4 SSQ SSJ SS2

notes: West leads the ♠J against 4♥. When East wins his ♠A and switches to a club, right into dummy's powerful holding, South should worry about East having been dealt a singleton club.
South is in danger of losing tricks to the ♥K and ♦K in addition to the ♠A. South can afford to lose those 3 tricks, but he cannot afford to have West give East a club ruff as well.

South should cash the ♥A and concede a heart trick to the ♥K. East wins the ♥K and returns a diamond. East has a trump left, making the diamond finesse too dangerous. Should that finesse lose to the ♦K in West, a club ruff will defeat the contract.
Taking an early heart finesse would be wrong as well. If West was dealt the ♥K, East may get a club ruff, leaving the fate of the contract dependent on the diamond finesse.

review.hl: EHK EH3 EH2 WC9 WC8 WC7
NHQ NHJ NHT NH9 SHA SH8 SH7 SH6 SH5

notes: South has a possible loser in both hearts and diamonds. West's spade lead has knocks out dummy's only entry. South must decide whether to finesse in hearts or diamonds.

If South takes the heart finesse, he may not be out of the woods, even if East has the ♥Q. East may have started with 4 or 5 hearts, in which case he will still get a heart trick. South will have to hope that East or West has a singleton ♦K. If the heart finesse loses, South will again need a miracle in diamonds.
South should take the diamond finesse at trick 2. If that finesse works, South can give up a trick to the ♥Q, if necessary, and take the rest of the tricks.
If the diamond finesse loses, South may still make his contract when the ♥Q drops doubleton or singleton.

review.hl: NH3 NH2 SHA SHK SHJ SHT SH9 SH8
NDT ND9 ND8 ND7 ND6 SDA SDQ

notes: West leads the ♦8 which South wins. South must simply find the ♣Q to make his grand slam. South may have to guess which opponent has the ♣Q. By playing 3 rounds of spades, hearts, and diamonds before tackling clubs, South may be able to turn a guess into a sure thing.

South will see West show out on the third round of spades. East will show out on the third rounds of hearts and diamonds. East's distribution is thus known to be 5 spades, 2 hearts, 2 diamonds, and 4 clubs. South should cash the ♣K and then pass the ♣10 with complete assurance. West is known to have no clubs left.

If South cannot obtain a complete count on the hand, he should do the best he can. South should play off the other three suits first and note any discards made. South should play the defender who appears long in clubs (if either one does) to have the ♣Q.

NSA NSQ NSJ SSK SS3 SS2 WS8 WS7
NHA NHQ NHJ EHT EH9 SHK SH3 SH2

notes: When South gains the lead in hearts, he cannot afford to play on spades. The defense would win the ♠A and cash enough heart tricks to defeat the contract.

South must hope to take 2 diamond tricks and 6 club tricks (along with his ♥A). South's best hope is that West has both the ♦K and ♣K. South must manage his single hand entry carefully so that he can take all of his finesses.
If South plays on clubs first, he may find himself locked in the dummy and unable to take the diamond finesse. South must play on diamonds first to best take advantage of the single hand entry.
If West ducks South's diamond play, the lead remains in the closed hand to play clubs. South starts by playing the ♣Q. West ducks, but South remains in his hand to take a second finesse in clubs.
It would have done West no good to cover South's diamond play with the ♦K. South can win the ♦A and cross back to the South hand in diamonds. South can then play clubs as before.

review.hl: NS4 NS3 NS2 SSK SSQ SSJ SST

NCA NCJ NCT NC9 NC8 NC7 SCQ SC3 SC2
NDA ND2 SDQ SDJ SDT SD9
NCA NCJ NCT NC9 NC8 NC7 SCQ SC3 SC2

notes: West leads the ♠K against 3NT. Only 5 top tricks are available (the ♠A, 2 heart tricks, the ♦A, and the ♣A). A successful finesse in either diamonds or clubs would provide enough tricks for the contract.
As East may eventually gain the lead, South should hold up the ♠A until the third round in an effort to exhaust East's spades. East's discard on the third round marks the 6-2 spade break.

South should play on diamonds first, passing the ♦Q through West. It would be wrong to take the club finesse first. If West turns out to have the ♣K, the contract will fail immediately as West will cash his spades.
When the diamond finesse loses, South's chances of making the contract are still good. South now has 8 tricks, but South should not take the club finesse for trick 9.

South wins East's return and should guard against a singleton ♣K with West by cashing the ♣A, declining the finesse. If the ♣K does not drop, South will still succeed when East has the ♣K (the finesse would have also worked in this case). South loses only 4 tricks (2 spade tricks, the ♦K, and the ♣K).
If West was dealt the guarded ♣K, the contract could not have been made.

notes: After the defense takes the ♥A, and switches to diamonds, South's only possible losers are in the club suit. If South draws all of the trumps, he will go down anytime clubs break 4-1.

South can give himself an extra chance to make the contract by testing clubs after drawing only 2 rounds of trump. If both defenders follow to 2 rounds of clubs, South can draw the last trump and easily take the balance of the tricks.
The recommended line is critical when the defender with 4 clubs also has length in spades. In this case, South can cash a third round of clubs and ruff a club in the dummy.
South's hand will now be high. South can draw the last trump and take the rest of the tricks.

If South crosses in spades and takes the heart finesse, the contract will have almost no hope if West can win the ♥K. South will be unable to take advantage of East holding the ♣Q.

South does better to play clubs before hearts. By leading a low club from the dummy, South will immediately succeed when East has the ♣Q. If West wins the ♣J with the ♣Q, North's remaining spade entry can be used to take the heart finesse. The contract will succeed if either the ♥K or ♣Q is favourably placed.

notes: West's spade lead is taken by East with the ♠A. East's heart shift appears helpful, but South must be careful when West covers South's heart with the ♥K.
South appears to have 12 tricks, 2 spades, 3 hearts, 6 diamonds, and the ♣A. If South tries to take these 12 tricks, however, he will find himself taking only 8.
After winning the ♥A, the blockage in diamonds prevents South from enjoying dummy's long suit. South will be held to 2 diamond tricks. When clubs break badly, 3NT will fail.
The solution is to allow West to hold the ♥K at trick 2! This play limits South to only 2 heart tricks, but preserves the ♥A as an entry to dummy's diamonds.
West continues hearts but South can win in hand, unblock the ♦A and ♦K, and cross to the ♥A. South is able to run the diamonds and take 11 tricks.

notes: West cashes 2 diamond tricks and exits in hearts, dummy's ♥A winning. South must hold his trump losers to 1 in order to make the contract.

If trumps are 3-2 or if either opponent has a singleton spade honor, South can succeed easily by playing trumps from the top. With careful play, South can also guard against East holding 4 spades including the ♠Q and ♠J.

South should lead a trump from dummy to his ♠A or ♠K. While finessing spades on the first round would pick up 4 spades to the ♠Q and ♠J in East's hand, South would not be comfortable if the finesse lost. In this case, South would have to guess whether he should finesse spades again on the next round.

When both defenders follow with small spades, South should cross to the dummy in clubs before leading a second spade. When East follows small, South finesses, guarding against East holding all of the remaining spades.

This line of play is not without danger. West might be able to win the second spade trick and give East a club ruff. So it is possible that the recommended safety play will defeat the contract when trumps are 3-2.

The chances of East holding a singleton club along with West holding a doubleton spade honor are not as good as the chances of East holding 4 spades to the ♠Q and ♠J. South should therefore take the safety play in trumps.

notes: West's club opening lead is won by South with the ♣A. The hand is solid except for the ♠Q. South must avoid losing 2 trump tricks to make the slam.

If the contract was 7 spades it would be correct to cross to the dummy and finesse East for the ♠Q ("8 ever". This would be a poor play in a small slam as West could win the ♠Q and give East a ruff in the red suit that South crossed to dummy in.

An alternative is to cash the ♠A and ♠K and use the ♠J or ♠10 to drive out the ♠Q. The problem with this line is that if a defender was dealt 4 trumps, he will play a red suit after winning the ♠Q. South will be unable to return to his hand to draw trump and the defense might be able to ruff 1 of dummy's top winners.
The solution is to lead the ♠J or ♠10 immediately. If a defender holding 4 spades to the ♠Q ducks, South can simply cash the ♠A and ♠K. The defense will be held to one trump trick.
If the defense wins the ♠Q and plays a red suit, South can win in dummy. Dummy's remaining small trump provides a safe link to the South hand to draw the outstanding trumps.

NDA NDK NDQ ND6 ND5 NHK NHQ NH6

notes: West leads the ♦6 against 3NT. South has only 5 top tricks, the ♠A, 2 hearts, the ♦A, and the ♣A. There are finessing positions in spades, diamonds, and clubs which could provide extra tricks. South's long clubs are the most promising trick source.

If dummy's ♦Q is finessed at trick 1, the contract is in danger. East may win the ♦K and return a spade. South might as well finesse but West could win the ♠K and clear the suit. South will still need to establish his clubs. If West has the ♣K, making that finesse lose, the defense may be in a position to cash enough spade tricks to defeat the contract.
South was unlucky to lose 3 of 3 finesses, but South can guarantee the contract by taking the ♦A at trick 1. The ♣J is led for a finesse. If the ♣J holds, South continues with the ♣10.

In this way, South sets up at least 4 club tricks without losing the lead to East (who can switch to an unfriendly spade). If West has the ♣K he cannot profitably attack spades from his side of the table.
If West wins the ♣K and exits a diamond to the ♦Q and East's ♦K, East can play a spade. It is too late, however, as the ♦J is high and represents South's ninth trick.
If West exits in hearts instead of diamonds, South wins and plays diamonds himself. By playing this way, the contract is certain even if all 3 finesses lose.

If South plays the ♦Q or ♦J and West covers with the ♦K, there will be 4 diamond tricks whenever West began with 2 or 3 diamonds. If West started with 4 diamonds to the ♦K, he will still have a diamond stopper and the contract will go down. If West started with the singleton ♦K, East will have a diamond stopper and the contract will similarly fail.

Nothing can be done if West started with 4 diamonds to the ♦K. South should pick up West's singleton ♦K, however, with careful play. South should lead a low diamond, not the ♦Q or ♦J, on the first round of the suit.

If West started with a singleton ♦K, South can take 4 diamond tricks with ease. If West follows with a small diamond, the ♦10 is finessed. South can cross back to his hand and repeat the diamond finesse by leading the ♦Q or ♦J. South will still succeed if West began with 2 or 3 diamonds to the ♦K.

notes: West's heart lead drives out South's ♥A. There are only 6 top tricks, 2 spades, the ♥A, the ♦A, and 2 clubs. South must hope for diamonds to provide the 3 additional tricks that are required. South should plan to finesse West for the ♦K. If West has 2 or 3 diamonds the contract will be made easily.

South can guard against West holding a singleton ♦K by leading a low diamond (as opposed to the ♦Q or ♦J) on the first round of the suit. When West follows with the ♦K, South has no trouble taking 4 diamond tricks.

Due to the presence of the ♦7 in dummy, South has a stronger play available. South should start with the ♦Q or ♦J. This play will be immediately fatal if West began with a singleton ♦K. It is necessary, however, to start diamonds this way in the more likely event the East has a singleton ♦9 or ♦8.
If West covers with the ♦K, South wins the ♦A as East follows with a high spot card. South can cross back to his remaining diamond honor and finesse against West's high diamond spot card.

If West does not cover on the first round of diamonds, South must continue with his other diamond honor. If West ducks again, South can finesse the ♦10 on the third round. If West covers on the second round, South can win the ♦A, cross back to his hand and finesse against West's high spot card in diamonds.

On the previous deal, a singleton ♦K with West was the only 4-1 break that could be picked up. As the diamond spots in dummy are stronger on this deal, South must choose between picking up a singleton ♦K with West or picking up a singleton ♦9 or ♦8 with East. As there are 2 combinations that favor starting with a diamond honor (versus 1 combination for starting with a low diamond), it is correct to play the ♦Q or ♦J on the first round.
